paras: The Butte anti-Chinese lynching threats of December 1888 were crowd threats against Chinese residents of Butte, Montana Territory, after a white miner, John Braden, died of a saw wound from a Chinese woodcutter. One dispatch said a crowd chased a Chinese man to hang him, but local reports described only threats, and no one was harmed. A Chinese man arrested as the suspect was held about a week before witnesses testified he was the wrong man.

On Saturday, December 8, Braden, who had been drinking, was struck on the neck with a wood saw by a Chinese man cutting wood in an alley behind the St. Louis Restaurant. Braden's companions said he had only chucked the woodcutter under the chin, while other witnesses said Braden knocked him down or struck him repeatedly first. The woodcutter escaped, and Braden died of a spinal injury on December 9 according to the Butte Semi-Weekly Miner, or December 10 according to wire dispatches.

At the scene, the Leader's Butte correspondent wrote, a crowd hunted the fugitive, who would have been "torn in pieces" if found. The Miner reported "loud threats" of hanging Chinatown residents to make them reveal where he was, adding that nothing came of them.

After Braden's death, according to a Great Falls Leader dispatch, about 200 men gathered on Main street "with the intention of lynching a few heathens," and one crowd chased a Chinese man several blocks to hang him before he escaped. The Miner described instead rumors of reprisals by friends of the dead man, met by about fifty special constables posted around Chinatown. A Great Falls Tribune dispatch said Sheriff Lloyd had stationed officers on hearing that a mob would attack Chinatown, and that no violence was attempted.

On the evening of the coroner's verdict, officers took an arrested Chinese man to jail, followed by an "immense throng." A few cries of "Hang him!" were heard and there was talk of taking him from the jail, but the sheriff's guard was ready and no one touched him.

The closed-door coroner's jury found that Braden died of a wound inflicted with felonious intent, and the Tribune named the woodcutter as A. H. Chee; the sheriff offered a $50 reward. One dispatch said the arrested man was soon released, but later reports said he was arraigned on December 17 as Ah Hen and pleaded not guilty. At his preliminary examination before Judge Engel, Braden's companions and other witnesses testified that he was not the woodcutter, and he was discharged. No report of Ah Chee's capture, or of any arrest of crowd members, appears in the coverage.

The Butte Semi-Weekly Miner and the two Great Falls dailies covered the affair for two weeks. The Miner's editorial asked that the city not be "tarnished by mob violence," and its news column cited the Rock Springs affair and quoted police saying Chinese residents were "goaded to desperation" by hoodlums' insults. Yet its headline spoke of "Fooling With a Mongolian When He Has a Weapon Handy."

The Great Falls papers wrote of "heathens" and the "murderous Mongolian," and the Leader's correspondent mocked the woodcutter as "Celestial Love." Outside Montana, the St. Paul Daily Globe headlined "LYNCHING IS FEARED" and called Braden a "White Bully," and a Dakota weekly ran "Lynching of a Chinaman Probable." A syndicated summary in Montana, Minnesota and Dakota papers said Braden belonged to the "hoodlum element."

The chase appears only in the Leader's dispatch; the Miner said the threats came to nothing and the Tribune said no violence was attempted. The papers also differ on whether the arrest came on December 11 or 12, at a laundry on East Broadway or a cabin in Chinatown.

bases: Crowds threatened to hang Chinese residents and the fugitive woodcutter after Braden's death, and one dispatch reports a chase to hang a Chinese man (A2, A4, A6, A9, A11); no one was killed.

No one was killed: the chased man escaped (A2), the threats to Chinatown and the jail came to nothing (A4, A9, A11), and the arrested suspect was discharged by a court (A20); crowds of more than three acted to avenge Braden's death (A2, A7).

Threats and crowds against Chinese residents are reported by several independent sources (A3, A4, A6, A9, A11), but the chase to hang a Chinese man appears only in the Leader's dispatch (A2), while the local Miner says the threats came to nothing and a Tribune dispatch says no violence was attempted (A4, A11).

accounts.label: Butte Miner (local)

accounts.label: Other eyewitnesses
accounts.gist: Braden knocked the woodcutter down or struck him repeatedly and was returning with a piece of wood when he was hit.

framing.detail: The Butte Miner's editorial opposed mob violence, and its news column quoted police saying Chinese residents were 'goaded to desperation' by hoodlums' insults, under the headline 'The Consequence of Fooling With a Mongolian When He Has a Weapon Handy'.
The Great Falls Leader called the Chinese 'heathens' and mocked the woodcutter as 'Celestial Love', while printing an eyewitness account that Braden struck first.
The Great Falls Tribune headlined 'BUTTE EXCITED' and spoke of the 'murderous Mongolian' and 'the heathen', reporting police precautions.
The St. Paul Daily Globe headlined 'LYNCHING IS FEARED' and called Braden a 'White Bully' whom the Chinese man resented.
A syndicated summary in Montana, Minnesota and Dakota papers said Braden 'belonged' to the 'hoodlum element'; the Kimball Graphic ran 'Lynching of a Chinaman Probable'.

record_check.dossier: Threats ran from the assault on Dec. 8 through the arrest on Dec. 11 or 12; the Main street crowd and chase are in a Dec. 10 dispatch printed Dec. 11.

Braden was the man killed by the Chinese woodcutter, not the mob's target. The targets were an unnamed Chinese man (chased), Chinatown residents, the fugitive Ah Chee, and the arrested suspect Ah Hen.
Attempted according to the Leader alone (chase to hang); threatened according to the local Miner and the Tribune.
The fugitive was at large and the chased man was in the open; only the later threat to mob the jail involved a man in custody, and it came to nothing.
Threats corroborated; the pursuit rests on one dispatch.
No county is named in the coverage.

record_check.record: After word of John Braden's death from an assault by a Chinese man, a crowd of about 200 gathered on Main street intending to lynch Chinese, and one crowd chased a Chinaman several blocks to hang him; he escaped.
record_check.dossier: Should note that the chase is reported only by the Leader, that local reports describe threats that came to nothing, and that a later arrest drew cries of 'Hang him!'; the arrested man was discharged.

info: Braden was cut with a saw on the afternoon of Saturday, Dec. 8, 1888
Butte: assault in the alley between West Broadway and West Park street behind the St. Louis Restaurant; crowds on Main street; threats directed at Chinatown

John Braden was the man killed by the woodcutter, not a mob victim.
A Chinese woodcutter was accused of killing John Braden by striking him on the neck with a wood saw; witnesses differed on whether Braden had first struck him
Described as friends of the dead man, the 'hoodlum element' or 'rough element'; no one named
No one was lynched; Ah Chee was still at large as of Dec. 20
